fallback.text: Twenty diploid individuals carry 40 copies of a gene, half of them allele A. Each generation the 40 copies of the next generation are drawn at random from the parents' copies, so the frequency of A wanders up and down with no selection at all. Within a few hundred generations each population ends with A fixed (frequency 1) or lost (0): about half of 200 populations fix A, exactly as the starting frequency predicts, and the mean heterozygosity falls by a factor 1 − 1/2N = 0.975 every generation. In larger populations the wandering is slower, and with selection a favoured allele still fixes only with Kimura's probability, (1 − e^(−2Nsp))/(1 − e^(−2Ns)) for additive effects.
